readerTitle: How McDonald's menu outgrew its speed
caseNote: 실제 기업 (McDonald's 메뉴 확장과 축소, Walmart 품목 축소) + 가상 적용 (드라이브스루 카페, 동네 철물점 계산대)
insight: 기능의 비용은 하나씩 따로 생기지 않는다. 기존의 모든 것과 얽히면서 쌓이므로, 추가는 전체 시스템 기준으로 판단해야 한다.
misconception: 고객이 원하는 기능을 하나씩 더하면 제품은 점점 좋아진다. 하나하나가 작으면 합쳐도 작다.

sources.text: McDonald's corporate history: the 1948 Speedee Service System and short original menu
McDonald's announcements on All Day Breakfast (US, 2015) and temporary menu simplification (2020)
Industry press coverage of McDonald's menu size, drive-thru times and franchisee complaints (around 2013–2015)

factChecks.note: 1948년 McDonald 형제가 메뉴를 약 9개 품목으로 줄였다는 내용은 공식 역사 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "about nine items"로 적었습니다.
2000년대~2010년대 초 미국 메뉴가 크게 늘고 드라이브스루 시간이 느려졌다는 내용은 업계 조사(QSR Drive-Thru Study 등)와 언론 보도를 근거로 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 구체적 품목 수나 초 단위 수치는 확인 전까지 넣지 않았습니다.
가맹점주들이 메뉴 복잡성에 불만을 표했다는 보도(2015년 전후 가맹점주 설문)와 2015년 이후 일부 품목 축소, 2020년 팬데믹 중 메뉴 일시 축소(올데이 브렉퍼스트 중단 등)를 게시 전 확인하세요.
Walmart가 2009년 품목을 줄인 뒤 매출이 약해져 2011년 상당수 품목을 되돌렸다는 보도를 확인하세요. 카드에는 숫자 없이 "reportedly"로 적었습니다.

cards.title: How McDonald's menu outgrew its speed
body: In 1948, the McDonald brothers cut their menu to about nine items. A tiny menu let them serve food in moments, and that speed built an empire.
Decades later, the menu had grown so large that the company started cutting it again. Nobody had planned the bloat. It arrived one good idea at a time.

image.label: A short menu board slowly growing into a crowded one
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 항목 몇 개뿐인 깔끔한 메뉴판, 오른쪽으로 갈수록 항목이 빽빽해지는 메뉴판 세 개가 이어짐. 실제 브랜드 로고, 황금 아치, 상표 색 조합은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Five good ideas for your drive-thru café.
body: Your drive-thru café is known for getting cars through fast. This year, regulars asked for five new things: oat milk, a breakfast wrap, a smoothie, custom syrups and a kids' meal. Each one would probably sell.
Which question matters most before you add them?

options.text: Will enough customers buy each one?
options.feedback: Demand matters, but every item here passes that test. It tells you each idea is good on its own, not what five of them do together.

options.text: How cheap is each one to add?
options.feedback: Ingredients and a menu line look cheap. The real cost shows up as extra steps, stock and decisions for every order in the line.

options.text: What do all five do to the speed customers come for?
options.feedback: This judges the additions against the whole system. You may still add some, but you'll know what each one takes away.

cards.title: One reasonable addition at a time.
body: Over the 2000s and early 2010s, McDonald's in the US kept adding: wraps, specialty coffees, salads, more burgers, later custom burgers and all-day breakfast. Each answered a real customer wish or a rival's move.
But every item shared the same kitchens, crews and drive-thru lanes. Industry surveys reported slower drive-thru times, and franchise owners complained publicly about menu complexity.
From about 2015, the company began trimming items. In 2020 it cut the menu further to keep kitchens simple.

cards.title: Feature creep
body: **Feature creep** is the slow pile-up of additions to a product or service, each sensible alone, until together they hurt what customers valued most.

The trap is how decisions get made. Each addition is judged by itself: does someone want it, can we afford it? Almost everything passes. Nobody asks what the hundredth item does to the first ninety-nine.

image.label: Small blocks stacked until the tower leans
image.brief: 작은 블록이 하나씩 쌓여 탑이 됨. 블록마다 "wrap", "smoothie", "custom" 같은 짧은 라벨. 맨 아래 큰 블록 "Speed"가 무게에 눌려 금이 감.

cards.title: The cost lives in the connections.
body: An addition rarely costs only itself. It touches everything already there:
list: **More steps:** staff must learn, remember and switch between more tasks
**More decisions:** customers take longer to choose
**More stock:** more items to order, store and waste
**More ways to fail:** each new piece can break something old
cards.callout: Ten small costs that touch every order add up to one big cost.
cards.softwareNote: In software, each feature adds screens, settings and code that every later change must work around. Products slow down for users and for the team, even when every feature was requested.

cards.title: Creep happens anywhere things get added.
body: A hotel adds questions to check-in until the line backs up. A contractor's quote grows options until clients can't compare it. A weekly meeting gains agenda items until no decision gets made.
The pattern is the same. Additions are easy to approve and rarely removed. Without a regular look at the whole, the pile only grows.

cards.title: Cutting blindly can hurt too.
body: The cure for creep isn't cutting everything. In 2009, Walmart reportedly removed many items from its shelves to simplify stores. Shoppers who couldn't find what they came for went elsewhere, and the company later brought many items back.
Some additions are exactly what customers rely on. The test isn't "is it new?" but "does it serve the core customer more than it costs the whole system?"

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store checkout.
body: Over two years, your neighborhood hardware store added steps at the register: a loyalty sign-up question, an email receipt prompt, a charity round-up, a warranty offer and a survey card. Each made sense.
Now Saturday lines run out the door, and some customers leave their carts. What do you do?

options.text: Remove every added step and go back to basics
options.feedback: Lines get faster, but you may lose the loyalty data or warranty income that pays for itself. Cutting without measuring trades one blind spot for another.
It eases the line but adds staff cost, and every checkout stays slow. You treat the symptom while the creep keeps growing.

options.text: Time each step, keep those that earn their seconds, and move or merge the rest
options.feedback: You judge each step against the whole checkout, not alone. The survey can go on the receipt; the loyalty question can wait for repeat visits.

cards.title: Judge every addition by what it does to the whole.
body: Feature creep comes from good ideas approved one at a time. Watch the thing customers came for, and check it every time something is added.
**Try it today:** list everything you've added to your product, menu or process in the past year. Next to each, write what it costs the rest. Pick one to remove or merge.
